source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Hall_2015_TwoDecadesAdverseEffects.pdf, online-first version, pp. 1-17 (all pages read in a text extraction; pp. 3-5, 7-10 and Table 1 on p. 12 checked on rendered pages)

claims.note: Hall (2015) is the source for half of people who use daily (ref 42, van der Pol et al., 2013, a three-year prospective study of the transition from frequent use to dependence) and, with Hall & Degenhardt (2009), for one in six with adolescent onset (ref 39, a 2006 book chapter, although the sentence presents both figures as estimates from longitudinal studies). No definition of daily use or of dependence, follow-up period or adjustment is given with either figure. Internal inconsistency worth knowing: the abstract (p. 1) says around one in 10 people who use regularly develop dependence, whereas the body gives half of people who use daily, and the body, Table 1 and conclusions give 1 in 10 for everyone who has used.

anchors.locator: Adverse health effects of chronic cannabis use › Cannabis dependence, 2nd paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Presented as estimates from longitudinal studies: risk of dependence one in six among people who started in adolescence (ref 39, Anthony 2006 book chapter) and half of people who use daily (ref 42, van der Pol et al. 2013, three-year prospective study of people who used frequently). No definitions, follow-up period or adjustment given.

anchors.locator: What have we learned in 20 years? › Adverse effects of chronic use › Psychosocial outcomes, 1st bullet
anchors.extracted: Dependence risk around 1 in 10 of all people who use cannabis and 1 in 6 among those who start in adolescence.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Results
anchors.extracted: Around one in 10 people who use regularly develop dependence: this denominator contradicts the body (half of people who use daily, p. 5) and Table 1 (1 in 10 among people who have ever used, p. 12).

claims.note: Second-hand: the 9% (stated as the US estimate for the early 1990s) is cited to the 2006 book chapter (ref 39), and the comparison figures to the 1994 National Comorbidity Survey paper (ref 40) together with a 1999 Australian survey paper (ref 41, Hall, Teesson, Lynskey & Degenhardt); the numbers are the NCS ones rounded, so the claim's 'comparison figures from the 1990-92 survey' is right in substance. Reporting issues in the review: the abstract says one in 10 people who use regularly, against people who have ever used in the body, Table 1 and conclusions; Table 1 gives cohort studies as the level of evidence for the 1 in 10, although the figure comes from cross-sectional surveys. The review's 1993 predecessor used DSM-III dependence (p. 4).

anchors.locator: Adverse health effects of chronic cannabis use › Cannabis dependence, 2nd paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Cannabis abuse and dependence affected 1-2% of adults in the past year and 4-8% in their lifetime (refs 6, 39). Lifetime risk of dependence among people who have ever used estimated at 9% in the USA in the early 1990s (ref 39), against 32% nicotine, 23% heroin, 17% cocaine, 15% alcohol and 11% stimulants (refs 40, 41).

anchors.locator: Table 1, Dependence row; and What have we learned in 20 years? › Psychosocial outcomes, 1st bullet
anchors.extracted: Dependence: evidence +++, level of evidence cohort studies, strength 1 in 10 among people who have ever used; conclusions: around 1 in 10 of all people who use cannabis.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Results
anchors.extracted: Around one in 10 people who use regularly develop dependence (denominator differs from the body and Table 1, which refer to everyone who has used).

claims.note: Hall (2015) calls Mittleman et al.'s 4.8 a quadrupling, and its Table 1 gives 3-4-fold for myocardial infarction under cohort and case-control evidence, although the one estimate described is from a case-crossover study. The conclusion the claim attributes to it (cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of myocardial infarction) is on p. 12. The review also supports the claim's laboratory sentence (dose-related heart-rate rises with rapid tolerance in healthy young adults; angina in older adults with cardiovascular disease). Not in the claim: risks are said to be probably highest in older adults, while younger adults with undiagnosed heart disease may also be at risk, on the basis of case reports (200 cannabis-related hospitalisations in Toulouse, 2004-2007, with several heart attacks and a fatal stroke in young adults).

anchors.locator: Adverse health effects of long-term cannabis smoking › Cardiovascular effects, 2nd paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Evidence consistent with adverse cardiovascular effects in middle-aged and older adults. Case-crossover study of 3,882 patients with myocardial infarction (ref 131): use acutely quadrupled the risk in the hour after smoking. Prospective study of 1,913 of them (ref 132): dose-response between frequency of use and mortality over 3.8 years (no figures given). These support older laboratory studies of angina in patients with heart disease.

anchors.locator: Adverse health effects of long-term cannabis smoking › Cardiovascular effects, 1st paragraph (begins p. 9, right column)
anchors.extracted: In 1993, laboratory studies had shown dose-related heart-rate increases with tolerance developing rapidly in healthy young adults (reviews, refs 128, 129), and clinical evidence of angina in older adults with cardiovascular disease (ref 130).

anchors.locator: Adverse health effects of long-term cannabis smoking › Cardiovascular effects, 3rd paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Risks probably highest in older adults; younger adults with undiagnosed cardiovascular disease may also be at risk: case reports from 200 cannabis-related hospitalisations in Toulouse (2004-2007) with several myocardial infarctions and a fatal stroke in young adults with recent use and no other known risk factors (ref 133).

anchors.locator: Table 1, Cardiovascular disease row; and What have we learned in 20 years? › Physical health outcomes, 2nd bullet
anchors.extracted: Cardiovascular disease: evidence ++, cohort and case control, strength 3-4-fold for myocardial infarction. Conclusion: cannabis smoking by middle-aged adults probably increases the risk of myocardial infarction.

claims.note: Matches the sentence the claim attributes to Hall (2015). One point of emphasis: the review says under-reporting of use probably weakens (attenuates) the associations with poor birth outcomes; the claim lists under-counting among the caveats without saying which way it biases, so a reader may take it as a reason to doubt the association rather than as a reason it may be underestimated. The review's own conclusion is causal (maternal use modestly reduces birth weight, p. 12), stronger than the claim's association wording, which is appropriate. The 'one large study found no rise in birth defects' sentence (attributed to Hall & Degenhardt, 2009) is also here, with use measured by urine tests.

anchors.locator: Reproductive effects of cannabis use › Fetal development and birth defects, 2nd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: A meta-analysis of 1980s-1990s studies (ref 26) suggested regular use in pregnancy reduced birth weight, by less than tobacco smoking. Several large studies since (refs 27, 28) report an association with reduced birth weight, generally persisting after statistical control for other drug use (refs 25, 28, 29); some also reported shorter labour and more babies small for gestational age (ref 27).

anchors.locator: Reproductive effects of cannabis use › Fetal development and birth defects, 3rd paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Limitations: self-reported use in pregnancy typically low (2-6%); urine-test studies suggest considerable under-reporting, which probably attenuates associations with poor birth outcomes; it has often been difficult to adjust fully for cigarette smoking.

anchors.locator: Reproductive effects of cannabis use › Fetal development and birth defects, 1st paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Zuckerman et al. (ref 25): the most convincing failure to find more birth defects, in a large sample with substantial use measured by urinalysis rather than self-report.

anchors.locator: What have we learned in 20 years? › Adverse effects of acute use, 4th bullet; Table 1, Low birth weight row
anchors.extracted: Maternal use during pregnancy modestly reduces birth weight; Table 1: low birth weight, evidence ++, cohort studies, no size given.

claims.overstatement: Slight, on framing: the claim says the reviews give absolute figures only as calculations that assume the association is causal. Hall (2015) presents 7 rising to 14 in 1,000 as its best estimate of risk in people who do not use and in people who use regularly, without stating a causal condition for that sentence (the explicit causal assumption introduces the next sentence). Applying a doubling to a base rate does treat the association as the effect, so the claim's reading is defensible, but 'given as the review's best estimate, by applying a doubling to a base rate' would be closer.
claims.note: The base rate (7 in 1,000) is cited to a systematic review of the prevalence of schizophrenia (ref 102, Saha et al., 2005), applied to people who do not use cannabis and called the risk of developing a psychosis. Two further absolute illustrations on the same page are explicitly conditional and not in the claim: about 4,700 young men aged 20-24 in the UK would have to be dissuaded to prevent one case, if causal (ref 99); and a rise from 10% to 20% for people with an affected first-degree relative who use regularly, if risks are independent and multiplicative (ref 103). The review also supports the claim's core with Moore et al.'s pooled 1.4 (1.20-1.65) and 2.09 (1.54-2.84) and the Swedish conscript gradient. Its conclusions assert that the doubling is greater with a personal or family history and with first use in the mid-teens, without data in the body for the age effect; the claim's 'not shown' stands, but the editors may wish to note that this review asserts it.

anchors.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Psychosis and schizophrenia, 7th paragraph (begins at foot of left column)
anchors.extracted: 'Our best estimate is that the risk of developing a psychosis doubles': from about 7 in 1,000 in people who do not use (ref 102, a review of schizophrenia prevalence) to 14 in 1,000 in people who use regularly. Next sentences, explicitly conditional: if causal, about 4,700 men aged 20-24 in the UK would have to be dissuaded to prevent one case (ref 99); if risks are independent and multiplicative with genetic risk, risk with an affected first-degree relative would rise from 10% to 20% with regular use (ref 103).

anchors.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Psychosis and schizophrenia, 4th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Meta-analysis of longitudinal studies (ref 97): pooled OR 1.4 (95% CI 1.20-1.65) for psychotic symptoms or disorders with ever use; 2.09 (1.54-2.84) with regular use. Reverse causation addressed in some studies; a common cause harder to exclude because adjustment attenuated the association and no study assessed all confounders.

anchors.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Psychosis and schizophrenia, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (right column; the 3rd continues on p. 8)
anchors.extracted: Swedish conscripts (50,465; 15-year follow-up): 2.4 times as likely to be diagnosed with schizophrenia after trying cannabis by 18; 2.3 times after 10 or more occasions by 18, adjusted for psychiatric history by 18 and parental divorce. Zammit et al. (27-year follow-up): dose-response with frequency at 18, persisting after adjustment.

anchors.locator: What have we learned in 20 years? › Psychosocial outcomes, 2nd bullet, and right column, 2nd bullet; Table 1, Psychosis row
anchors.extracted: Regular use doubles the risk of psychotic symptoms and disorders, especially with a personal or family history of psychotic disorders and first use in the mid-teens; regular use in adolescence approximately doubles the risk of a schizophrenia diagnosis or psychotic symptoms in adulthood. Table 1: psychosis, 2-fold in regular use, cohort studies.

claims.note: Hall (2015) supplies the modelling and case-register descriptions, and for the general-practice study it cites the 2008 Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs report (ref 90), so 'known only through a 2008 government advisory report' holds for this review too. Of the reasons the claim gives for calling the evidence weak, this review supplies the modest size of any causal effect, changing diagnostic criteria and services, poor administrative data, and other changing influences (possible social improvements such as antenatal care); the point that individuals' use and illness are not linked is not in this review, and it speaks of trends being hidden, not created. No doubling figure for south-east London here.

anchors.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Psychosis and schizophrenia, 5th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Sceptics argue that no rise in schizophrenia incidence as use rose is inconsistent with causation. Mixed evidence: Australian modelling study (ref 98, Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey 2003) found no increased psychosis incidence after steep rises in use in the 1980s-1990s; British modelling study (ref 99): too early to detect an increase; case-register studies in Britain (ref 100, south-east London 1965-1999) and Switzerland (ref 101, Zurich) reported increased incidence in recent birth cohorts; a British study of people treated for schizophrenia in general practice did not (ref 90, Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, 2008).

anchors.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Psychosis and schizophrenia, 6th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Difficult to decide: even if causal, cannabis would produce a very modest increase in incidence; detection complicated by changes in diagnostic criteria and psychiatric services, poor administrative data on treated cases, and possibly social improvements (e.g. antenatal care) lowering incidence over the same period.

claims.note: Not supported as worded: the claim describes 'dose-response relations that lost significance after adjustment' in the Fergusson & Horwood cohort and in the Swedish conscript cohort. For the Swedish cohort, Hall (2015) reports a two-group contrast, not a dose-response: depression 1.5 times as common with the heaviest use at 18 as with no use, no longer significant after adjustment (ref 108). Suggested wording: '...in one birth cohort (frequency of use by 16), and an association that lost significance after adjustment in the Swedish conscript cohort (depression 1.5 times as common with the heaviest use at 18 as with none)'. The rest is supported: the link with depression is weaker than with psychosis (ref 107, a 2012 book chapter by the same group), OR 1.49 (1.15-1.94) with weak support for causation. Not in the claim: a combined analysis of four Australasian cohorts reached similar conclusions (ref 110), and Table 1 rates the evidence +? with probable confounding.

anchors.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Cannabis use and other mental disorders, 2nd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Since 1993 the relationship of regular use with depression has been weaker than with psychosis (ref 107). Swedish conscripts (ref 108): depression 1.5 times as common with the heaviest use at 18 as with none, not significant after adjustment. Fergusson & Horwood (ref 109): dose-response between frequency of use by 16 and depressive disorder, not significant after adjustment. Meta-analysis (ref 97): modest association, OR 1.49 (95% CI 1.15-1.94), weak support for causation because most studies had not adequately controlled confounding or excluded that depressed young people use more. Similar conclusions from four Australasian birth cohorts (ref 110).

anchors.locator: Table 1, Depression row
anchors.extracted: Depression: evidence +?, cohort studies, probable confounding.

claims.note: Editors' calculation recomputed (crude OR about 9.3 from 16% and 2%, about 9.1 from the implied counts, about 7 to 13 given rounding): 'about 9' is right. The ideation result (van Ours et al., 2013) is an econometric re-analysis of the same Christchurch cohort as the Fergusson & Horwood result, so the two are not independent; the 'fourth' study (Rasic et al., 2013) was of Nova Scotia high-school students. Not in the claim: a Norwegian registry study of 6,445 people treated for cannabis use disorder found suicide OR 5.3 (3.3-7.79), 4.8 (2.4-8.9) after excluding people known to inject (adults in treatment; limited confounder control); and Table 1 summarises suicide as +? evidence with a 2-fold risk in regular use. The text's mixed picture supports the claim; the table's 2-fold figure is the review's own summary and could be mentioned.

anchors.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Cannabis use and other mental disorders, 4th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: New Zealand case-control study of suicide attempts resulting in hospitalisation (ref 116): 16% of 302 people who attempted suicide had a cannabis disorder against 2% of 1,028 community controls; adjustment for social disadvantage, depression and alcohol dependence substantially reduced but did not eliminate the association (adjusted OR 2).

anchors.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Cannabis use and other mental disorders, 5th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Prospective evidence mixed: Fergusson & Horwood (ref 109), dose-response between frequency by 16 and self-reported attempts not persisting after adjustment; van Ours et al. (ref 117), econometric re-analysis of that cohort, more than weekly use increased reported suicidal ideation in males only; Patton et al. (ref 118), self-harm in females only; Rasic et al. (ref 119), heavy use increased depression but not suicide risk; attempted meta-analysis (ref 97): designs and measures too varied to quantify risk.

anchors.locator: Cannabis use and mental health › Cannabis use and other mental disorders, 6th paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Norway, 6,445 people treated for cannabis use disorder (ref 120): suicide OR 5.3 (CI 3.3-7.79); 4.8 (2.4-8.9) after excluding people known to inject; case registers, limited control for confounders.

anchors.locator: Table 1, Suicide row
anchors.extracted: Suicide: evidence +?, cohort studies, 2-fold in regular use.

claims.note: Supports 'often severe enough to impair everyday life' (ref 45, Allsop et al., 2012), and is also the source of the ranking that the claim attributes to Hall & Degenhardt (2009): the most common withdrawal symptoms include anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression (ref 44). The same paragraph describes a double-blind controlled trial (ref 46, Allsop et al., 2014) in which nabiximols (Sativex; called an oral extract here, though it is an oromucosal spray) markedly attenuated withdrawal symptoms, a randomized result relevant to the claim's second-hand statement that THC relieves the symptoms.

anchors.locator: Adverse health effects of chronic cannabis use › Cannabis dependence, 3rd paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: Evidence for a withdrawal syndrome strengthened since 1993; tolerance to THC in laboratory studies (ref 43); people seeking help often report withdrawal symptoms that make abstinence harder; the most common include anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression (ref 44), often severe enough to impair everyday functioning (ref 45); a double-blind controlled trial found them markedly attenuated by nabiximols (ref 46).

key_findings.correction: The review says the 1980s-1990s meta-analysis suggested (not found) that regular use in pregnancy reduced birth weight (p. 3). Add from p. 4: under-reporting of use probably attenuates the associations with poor birth outcomes, and cigarette smoking has often been hard to adjust for fully.

key_findings.note: Refs 64 (Campbell et al. 1971), 65 (Hirvonen et al., title 'Reversible ...'), 68 (Baker et al. 2013) and 69 (Batalla et al. 2013) checked.

key_findings.correction: The finding is right; the note is not. School leaving is not the review's only discordant-twin test of a causal claim: the Other drug use section (p. 7) reports discordant-twin studies (Lynskey et al. 2003; US and Dutch studies, both cited to ref 86) in which the association with other illicit drug use persisted within pairs. School leaving is the only such test that went against the causal reading.

key_findings.note: Agrees with my blind reading: the 7 in 1,000 base comes from a review whose title concerns schizophrenia prevalence, and the sentence itself carries no explicit causal condition (the next one does).
Could add the review's framing sentences (p. 10): the evidence is consistent with adverse effects in middle-aged and older adults, and the risks are probably highest in older adults.
Ref 142 is Hashibe et al. 2005. The note's figures from card sc_callaghan_2013 cannot be checked from this source.
Refs 154 (Daling et al. 2009), 155 (Lacson et al.) and 156 (Trabert et al. 2011) checked.
Refs 164 (Swift et al.) and 165 (Wittchen et al.) checked.

risk_of_bias.note: Checked: 16 references name Hall, 13 as an author (refs 2, 6, 9, 11, 41, 49, 51, 70, 84, 98, 107, 157, 163) and 3 chapters in a book he co-edited (refs 14, 134, 139), as the card says; Rogeberg (2013) is not cited; literature searches are mentioned only in the acknowledgements. The citation-instance counts (31 of 225) were not rechecked.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract and Table 1 state doublings (cognition, school leaving) and a dependence denominator that the body does not support.

missed: Pregnancy (KF 5): the review's statement that under-reporting probably attenuates the associations, and that cigarette smoking is often hard to adjust for fully (p. 4). The claim cl_can_pregnancy_birth uses both points, the first without its direction.

The family-history qualifier in the psychosis conclusion (p. 12) repeats a 1993 conclusion listed among the acute effects on pp. 2-3 (psychotic symptoms at high doses, especially with a personal or family history of psychosis); no new evidence for it is presented, which supports the card's note on KF 27.
